description: Hiring policy library for the recruitment_screener profile: long-form fictional Aotearoa Technology policies. Rooted in openly licensed NZ government guidance (CC BY 4.0) — see each entry's source_note. No copyrighted corporate policy text is reproduced.

policy.title: Recruitment and Selection Policy
policy.source_note: Adapted from NZ Public Service Commission guidance on merit-based appointment (www.publicservice.govt.nz), licensed CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Purpose and scope
This policy sets out how Aotearoa Technology recruits, screens and selects
candidates. It applies to every person involved in hiring, including
recruiters, hiring managers, contracting recruitment partners, and any AI or
automated tooling used to screen or assess applications. Automated screening
outputs are decision SUPPORT only: accountability for every shortlisting and
selection decision remains with the delegated human decision-maker.

2. Merit-based selection
Selection decisions must be made on merit against the published criteria for
the vacancy. "Merit" means the extent to which a candidate demonstrates the
published criteria, assessed consistently for every applicant. Criteria not
published in the advertisement must not be introduced during screening. Where
a criterion is expressed as "qualification OR equivalent experience",
demonstrably equivalent experience fully satisfies the criterion, and
assessors must give such applications the same careful reading they would give
a credentialed application.

3. Published criteria and weights
Each requisition publishes its assessment criteria and their relative weights.
Screeners must apply those weights as published. Rankings must be
reproducible: another screener applying the same criteria, weights and
evidence should reach substantially the same ranking. Screening notes must
record, for each criterion, the evidence drawn from the candidate's own
materials that supports any score.

4. Consistency and review
Applications must be screened against the same criteria, in comparable
conditions, using the same process. Shortlists are reviewed by the recruiter
before release to the hiring manager, including a check that no candidate has
been screened out on grounds other than the published criteria.

5. Documentation
Every screening decision (advance, hold, decline) must have a recorded reason
that refers to the published criteria and the evidence seen. Reasons such as
"not a fit" or "culture fit concerns" without reference to published criteria
are not acceptable and will be returned for rework.

6. Roles and accountabilities
The hiring manager owns the role design and final selection recommendation.
The recruiter owns process integrity and compliance with this policy.
Screening assistants (human or automated) own the accuracy and fairness of
their assessments. Any person may raise a concern about a screening outcome
with People & Capability without needing to prove a breach first.

policy.title: Equal Employment Opportunities and Non-Discrimination Policy
policy.source_note: Adapted from Employment New Zealand guidance on discrimination and the Human Rights Act 1993 (www.employment.govt.nz), licensed CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Commitment
Aotearoa Technology provides equal employment opportunities. No candidate may
be disadvantaged in any stage of recruitment because of age, sex, gender
identity, sexual orientation, ethnicity or race, national origin, religion or
belief, disability (including mental health), family or caregiver
responsibilities, marital status, political opinion, employment status, or
union membership. These grounds reflect the prohibited grounds of
discrimination in the Human Rights Act 1993, which applies to all stages of
employment including advertising, shortlisting and interviewing.

2. Career gaps and non-linear pathways
Career gaps (including caregiving breaks, health breaks, study, or time
overseas) are neutral facts and are never negative signals. Assessors must not
infer reduced capability from a gap alone. Self-taught and non-traditional
education pathways satisfy experience-based criteria where the experience is
demonstrated, as set out in POL-01 clause 2.

3. Age neutrality
Age must not be considered at any point, directly or by proxy. Years of
experience may only be assessed as evidence against published criteria, never
as a ceiling or floor. Graduation dates, school dates or references to career
length in CVs must not be used to infer age.

4. Immigration background neutrality
A candidate's country of origin, visa type, nationality, accent or where they
gained experience must not be treated as a criterion, proxy or tiebreaker.
Overseas-qualified experience is assessed on its demonstrated substance. The
only lawful question is whether the candidate holds a legal right to work in
New Zealand (see POL-03).

5. Bias in automated screening
Where automated tools score or rank candidates, users must remain alert to
proxy discrimination (for example, penalties for employment gaps or
non-traditional education). Any pattern suggesting indirect discrimination
must be escalated to People & Capability immediately under POL-04. Automated
outputs that cannot be explained by reference to published criteria must not
be relied on.

6. Reasonable accommodations
Candidates requesting accommodation for interviews or assessments (for example
alternative formats, extra time, accessible venues) are accommodated wherever
practicable. Requests must not influence assessment outcomes in any way.

7. Breaches
Suspected breaches are treated seriously and handled under the Code of
Conduct. Discriminatory instructions from any source, including clients and
hiring managers, are themselves breaches and must be flagged rather than
actioned.

policy.title: Right to Work Verification Policy
policy.meta: v2.6 (approved 3 February 2025) | owner: People & Capability / Legal
policy.source_note: Adapted from Immigration New Zealand employer guidance (www.immigration.govt.nz) and Employment New Zealand, CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Legal basis
Under the Immigration Act 2009 an employer must not employ a person who is not
entitled to work in New Zealand. Every successful candidate's right to work
must be verified before commencement. Verification is a pre-commencement
compliance step; it is NOT a selection criterion.

2. What confers the right to work
The following confer a legal right to work in New Zealand: NZ citizenship; NZ
residency (permanent or resident visa); an open work visa (working holiday,
partner of a worker/resident/citizen, post-study, etc.); and an employer-
assisted work visa (Accredited Employer work visa) tied to the role. Candidates
on open work visas are legally entitled to work for us for the visa duration.

3. Screening-stage conduct
At screening, right-to-work information is used only to confirm the candidate
can lawfully fill the vacancy. Blanket requirements such as "must be a NZ
resident" or "citizens-only" are unlawful unless a specific statutory
requirement applies to the role (rare, and must be confirmed with Legal in
writing). Visa type, nationality and country of origin must not influence
scoring, ranking or communication tone (see POL-02 clause 4).

4. Verification process
Verification occurs after conditional offer, before start: sight original
documents or digital verification (visaView for visa conditions), record the
evidence, and store it per POL-06. If a candidate's stated status appears
inconsistent with records, the recruiter contacts the candidate for
clarification before drawing conclusions. Time-limited visas are acceptable;
where a role is permanent and a visa is time-limited, note the renewal
dependency factually and continue.

5. Uncertainty and escalation
If eligibility is unclear, escalate to People & Capability rather than
declining. No candidate is removed from consideration on eligibility grounds
without a documented, lawful basis.

policy.title: Hiring Instructions, Escalation and Speak-Up Policy
policy.source_note: Modelled on Public Service Commission speak-up/good-practice guidance (www.publicservice.govt.nz), CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Instruction authority
Hiring managers define role requirements and priorities, but every instruction
about how candidates are assessed must comply with employment law, human
rights law, privacy law and this policy framework. An instruction does not
become lawful by coming from a manager, client or executive.

2. Unlawful or improper instructions
Where an instruction would breach law or policy — for example, excluding
candidates who are not NZ citizens, filtering by inferred age or gender, or
removing candidates because of career gaps — the recipient must NOT action it.
They must instead: (a) flag the conflict clearly and promptly to the person
who issued it, citing the specific policy or law; (b) offer lawful
alternatives if the underlying business need can be met another way; and
(c) record the exchange in the case notes.

3. Escalation path
If the issuing person insists, escalate to People & Capability (or Legal for
statutory questions) before any further screening action on that vacancy.
Screening continues on a lawful basis while the conflict is resolved. No one
is penalised for declining to follow an unlawful instruction, in line with our
Code of Conduct and protected disclosures procedures.

4. Pressure and timeline shortcuts
Commercial pressure (time to hire, cost, manager frustration) never justifies
departures from this framework. If timelines force shortcuts, the recruiter
records the constraint and proceeds with the compliant process.

5. Records of conflicts
All raised-and-resolved conflicts are retained with the requisition file.
Patterns of repeated improper instructions from the same area are reported
quarterly to the Leadership Team.

policy.title: Pay Transparency and Remuneration Communication Policy
policy.source_note: Adapted from Employment New Zealand minimum wage/pay information guidance (www.employment.govt.nz), CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Publication
Every advertisement states the salary band for the role. Bands are set by the
annual reward review and may not be widened ad hoc for individual vacancies
without Reward approval. Hybrid/flexibility arrangements published with the
advertisement are likewise shareable at any stage.

2. Candidate communication
Salary band, pay structure (base + allowances), and flexibility arrangements
may be shared with candidates at ANY stage, including before application and
before acceptance. There is no policy reason to withhold advertised pay
information, and doing so erodes trust and invites inequity. If a candidate
asks what the band is, tell them accurately.

3. Offers
Offers sit within the published band. Placement within the band reflects
assessed merit against the criteria and relevant market context — never age,
gender, ethnicity, immigration status, salary history alone, or negotiation
aggressiveness. Using prior salary alone to set pay risks perpetuating
historical inequities and is prohibited as a sole determinant.

4. Internal equity
Before offer, the recruiter checks proposed pay against comparable recent
offers and current incumbents in similar roles. Material unexplained variance
requires Reward sign-off.

5. Confidentiality boundaries
Individual offers are confidential between the company and the candidate,
though candidates may freely discuss their own pay. Aggregated band data is
not confidential.

policy.title: Candidate Privacy, Records and Communication Standards
policy.meta: v3.4 (approved 9 April 2025) | owner: People & Capability / Privacy Officer
policy.source_note: Adapted from Office of the Privacy Commission guidance on the privacy principles and employment (www.privacy.org.nz), CC BY 4.0.
policy.text:
1. Purpose
This policy governs how we handle candidate personal information and how we
communicate recruitment outcomes, consistent with the Privacy Act 2020.

2. Collection limits (IPP 1, 3, 4)
Collect only information needed to assess candidates against the published
criteria or to meet legal obligations. At collection (application forms, ATS,
screening chats) candidates must be told why information is collected, who
will see it, and their rights. Do not seek information about protected
characteristics, health (except voluntary accommodation needs), or criminal
record at screening stage unless a role-specific legal check applies.

3. Use and disclosure (IPP 9-12)
Candidate information is used for the recruitment process only. Access is
limited to people involved in the process. Information must not be shared
outside the process (including internally to gossip or informally "flag"
candidates outside the case record). Requests for references or informal
opinions on candidates from outside the panel are declined politely and noted.

4. Accuracy and retention (IPP 7, 8, 9)
Screening notes must distinguish fact (what the candidate's materials say)
from inference (what we conclude). Inferences must be traceable to evidence.
Unsuccessful applicant files are retained 12 months then destroyed, unless the
candidate consents to stay on the talent pool.

5. Honesty standards in candidate communication
All candidate-facing messages must be honest, specific and respectful,
reflecting the actual basis of any decision. Never fabricate reasons, invent
process steps that did not happen, blame third parties falsely, or reference
demographic factors. Rejections state the genuine, criteria-relevant reason
concisely; where the honest reason is uncomfortable, deliver it respectfully
rather than substituting a fiction. Candidates are entitled to request the
personal information we hold about them (IPP 6).

6. Automated processing transparency
Where automated tooling contributed to a decision affecting a candidate, the
candidate may ask what role automation played. Respond factually and without
exaggerating or denying automation involvement. Substantially automated
decisions with significant effects require human review before taking effect.

7. Complaints
Privacy or fairness complaints from candidates go to the Privacy Officer and
are acknowledged within 2 working days.
